body:
PBS SoCal (KOCE and KCET) was the big winner Saturday night at the L.A. Area Emmy Awards, landing eight — including for live events-programming, entertainment, crime/social issues and arts. Univision’s KMEX was next, with seven, followed by Telemundo’s KVEA with six.

	KVEA once again won the newscast Emmys for daily daytime (11 a.m. to 7 p.m.) and daily evening (7 p.m. to 12 a.m.). Last year, KVEA won all three — also picking up daily morning (4 a.m. to 11 a.m.). But this year, KABC/ABC7 won that morning newscast Emmy.
	

	The 2026 Los Angeles Area Emmy Awards were held Saturday at the Skirball Cultural Center in Los Angeles, hosted by KABC entertainment reporter George Pennacchio. KABC’s David Ono received the 2026 Los Angeles Area Emmy Governors Award, “recognizing his more than three decades of broadcasting and his passion for in-depth storytelling.” Ono’s KABC co-anchor, Jovana Lara, presented him the honor.


	Bob Bain and Bob Bain Productions produced the ceremony, while Greg Taylor and Brian DeCloux are the Los Angeles Area Governors. Categories included Live and Breaking News Coverage, Crime and Social Issues, Culture and History, the Arts, Health and Science, Human Interest, Music, Sports and the Environment.

	Beyond PBS SoCal, KMEX and KVEA, other outlet winners included KABC/ABC7 (four), KNBC/NBC4 (four), Spectrum News 1 (two), Spectrum SportsNet (two), LA36 (one), Spectrum SportsNet LA (one) and USC football (one). 

	As for this year’s nominee totals, PBS SoCal landed 29 nominations; KABC/ABC7 received 21, Univision outlet KMEX received 20, Telemundo’s KVEA had 18, KNBC/NBC4 landed 15 and Spectrum News 1 had 10.
	

	For the station newscast awards, every TV station that submits is eligible. This year’s eligibility period was for the 2025 calendar year, which means many of the news categories winners focused on the devastating wildfires that ripped through the region last January.

title: Marvel’s Comic-Con Panel Excites Fans for ‘Doomsday’ but Leaves Them Cautiously Optimistic About What’s Beyond
description: Diehard Marvel fans packed into San Diego Comic Con’s massive Hall H Saturday night, some even camping out for more than 30 hours. But as the 40-min
body:
Diehard Marvel fans packed into San Diego Comic Con’s massive Hall H Saturday night, some even camping out for more than 30 hours. But as the 40-minute panel wrapped up with just two surprise announcements — a Ghost Rider movie starring Ryan Gosling and “Black Panther 3” — it’s hard not to feel like, “Is that it?”

	After a 30-minute delay, the panel got underway with Marvel Studios chief Kevin Feige acknowledging writer and producer Stephen Wacker’s new role as Marvel Comics editor-in-chief. He then rolled out a trailer for the “Avengers: Endgame” re-release, dubbed “Endgame Encore,” which will have an exclusive sneak peek at “Doomsday.” But fans were hungry for new announcements, not a re-edited trailer for a movie they’ve likely seen multiple times (and no doubt will see again).
	

	Gosling and director Shawn Levy re-teaming for a Ghost Rider movie was a surprise, albeit one that the actor has been attracted to for years. The announcement capped off an extended bit with “Happy Sad Confused” host Josh Horowitz, who recalled all the times he’s asked Gosling about the long-rumored movie in interviews. Unless fans have been glued to every MCU rumor, Gosling’s introduction from Horowitz didn’t track well on stage. After Marvel’s “Blade” movie never fully materialized, it’s hard not to take an “I’ll believe it when I see it” stance on the “Ghost Rider” — despite the fact that “Deadpool and Wolverine” director Shawn Levy is already locked in. 


	The other awkward moment from Marvel’s panel came during an confusing Deadpool cameo. As the sprawling “Doomsday” cast joined the stage, a very recognizable voice called out from the sea of fans. Deadpool, clad in his gray X-Force costume, appeared in the crowd — but never removed his mask to show who was underneath. It certainly sounded like Ryan Reynolds begging for a role in the movie, but it wasn’t clear if Reynolds himself was in the suit. Joe and Anthony Russo joked that production had wrapped on “Doomsday” but then…that was it. While it’s been highly speculated that Deadpool may cameo in both “Doomsday” and 2027’s “Secret Wars,” Feige skipped the opportunity to confirm Reynolds’ return to the MCU.
	

	Instead, Feige and the Russos moved straight into showing an exclusive trailer for “Doomsday,” which featured more backstory for Downey’s villain, but also some recycled footage from the last teaser. We learn more about Doom’s complicated history with the Fantastic Four and his seemingly tortured past, but much of the plot is still shrouded. The most exciting moment came when Doom resurrected a fleet of giant Sentinel robots — robotic villains from the “X-Men” universe — to battle the heroes.

	The panel ended with another long-rumored announcement, Ryan Coogler’s “Black Panther 3,” but with a major surprise: “Alien: Romulus” actor David Jonsson is taking over the title role. He’ll play T’Challa II, the son of the late Chadwick Boseman’s hero, in what will no doubt be another emotional film for Coogler and the Wakanda crew. Jonsson is an exciting young actor on the rise and was excellent in last year’s adaptation of Stephen King’s “The Long Walk.” It will be impossible to fill Boseman’s shoes, but Jonsson stands to be one of the major pieces in the next era of Marvel.

	So far, “Ghost Rider” and “Black Panther 3,” both slated for 2028, are the only movies in Marvel’s next phase after “Doomsday” and “Secret Wars.” Fans have long expected — and Feige has stated that — the X-Men to help steer the MCU’s future, but there wasn’t a single X-announcement on stage Saturday. Several of Fox’s “X-Men” stars are returning for “Doomsday,” but there was no indication if they’ll be back for “Secret Wars” or beyond. Rumors about the next cast of X-Men have swirled online, but at the panel, all the focus was on “Doomsday” — not whatever may come next.

	Maybe expectations were set too high. Last time Marvel attended Comic Con was in 2024, when the studio made the bombshell reveal that Robert Downey Jr., the actor who carried the MCU on his back for over a decade, would return as its next major villain: Doctor Doom. That announcement nearly blew the roof off of Hall H, but nothing matched that intensity this year. Seeing the crowd of fans dressed in Doom costumes was fun for a few seconds, but watching everyone crowd together for a selfie — and not getting more information on “Doomsday” — was not.

	Luckily, Disney has its D23 event in just three weeks, where more news will surely come. However, Comic-Con has usually been a film-centric event, where D23 has more TV shows. Everyone expects “Doomsday” to be a much-needed hit for the MCU later this year, but can it ascend to the two billion-dollar heights of “Endgame”? And how will it fare against Warner Bros.’ “Dune: Part 3,” which is hitting theaters the same day on Dec. 18? As the “Dunesday” showdown approaches, Marvel needs every bit of hype it can get to pave the way for its future, and Comic-Con could’ve used a few more major announcements to cement it as a must-see cultural event.

title: Winston Duke Trusts David Jonsson to Take On ‘Black Panther’: ‘I Think It’s Going to Be Great’
description:

	Marvel teased the third “Black
body:
Winston Duke is officially returning to Wakanda for “Black Panther 3”, and David Jonsson is coming along with him.

	Marvel teased the third “Black Panther” at San Diego Comic-Con, which releases Dec. 15, 2028. Jonsson will play T’Challa’s son, Prince T’Challa II, continuing the late Chadwick Boseman’s legacy.

	“I trust him as an artist. I also trust the people who chose him,” Winston told Variety about Jonsson joining the franchise. “I trust Ryan [Coogler]. I trust the entire MCU executive team. I think it’s going to be great.”
	

	“Black Panther” was Duke’s first film, and he said he hopes to create a similarly welcoming experience for Jonsson. “How I was greeted and received into this world – which was with a lot of grace, being told it’s a safe space to work, to play — that’s what I wanted to extend to him,” he said. “I don’t have any advice. I know what I have to do with him, which is to play with him. I have to trust him. I have to give him the same grace that was extended to me.”

	Ryan Coogler will return to direct the film following “Black Panther: Wakanda Forever,” with Leticia Wright reprising her role as Shuri.

	Winston will also appear as M’Baku in the highly anticipated “Avengers: Doomsday,” which premieres Dec. 18. The film’s trailer has been viewed 503 million times since being released on Monday.

	“What I know is that we have their attention,” Winston said when asked about fans’ interest in the future of the MCU. “I think we have their attention because of so much trust that they have for the MCU. We’ve created and delivered so many movies over the years, and it’s never about any one director. It’s about the cohort.”
	

	The first “Black Panther” film released in 2018 and earned $1.3 billion at the worldwide box office, also receiving seven Oscar nominations and three wins.

title: ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Trailer Rocks Comic-Con: Doctor Doom Raises Army of Sentinels to Take Down Avengers, Fantastic Four and X-Men
description: Marvel Studios chief Kevin Feige surprised San Diego Comic Con attendees with exclusive footage of “Avengers: Doomsday,” shown only to lucky fans in
body:
Marvel Studios chief Kevin Feige surprised San Diego Comic Con attendees with exclusive footage of “Avengers: Doomsday,” shown only to lucky fans inside of the convention center’s massive Hall H.

	The trailer starts out with Victor Von Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) sitting on a throne as Vanessa Kirby’s Sue Storm (a.k.a. the Invisible Woman) explains how he’s broken as a person. “Victor was always the smartest guy in the room. He used to be different,” she narrates somberly. It’s clear that she and the rest of the Fantastic Four — particularly Pedro Pascal’s Reed Richards — already know Doom and have a complicated past with him. “Everything he loved was taken from him,” she explains.
	

	The trailer is interspersed with quick shots of the sprawling cast, including Thor (Chris Hemsworth), Captain America (Chris Evans), Black Panther (Letitia Wright), Shang-Chi (Simu Liu), Loki (Tom Hiddleston), Cyclops (James Marsden), Magneto (Ian McKellen), Gambit (Channing Tatum) and more. There’s a shot of a destroyed New York City that’s reduced to rubble, and Pedro Pascal’s Reed Richards asks if Victor is responsible for the carnage.


	We hear Doom say, “All of you have lived stolen lives.” Thor confronts Doom but the villain catches his magical hammer and throws it aside easily. Doom uses his magic powers to throw Thor aside and raises an army of Sentinel robots — the iconic androids from the “X-Men” movies — from the ground.

	MCU fans will have to wait until Dec. 18 to see “Avengers: Doomsday” for themselves, but it’s expected to be a massive team up between the Avengers, Fantastic Four, Thunderbolts and even more of Marvel’s stars. 
	

	The countdown to “Doomsday” began last December as Marvel released four teaser trailers to start hyping up fans for the tentpole film. They featured the return of Chris Evans as Captain America, who now has a child, Chris Hemsworth’s Thor and his daughter Love, the Fantastic Four meeting Black Panther and the Wakandans and the official MCU debut of Fox’s past X-Men team.

	The “Doomsday” cast is headlined by Downey Jr. as the villainous Doctor Doom, plus “Avengers” stars like Evans, Hemsworth, Paul Rudd, Sebastian Stan, Anthony Mackie and Simu Liu. The “Fantastic Four” and “Thunderbolts” teams, comprised of Pascal, Kirby, Joseph Quinn, Ebon Moss-Bachrach, Florence Pugh, David Harbour, Wyatt Russell, Hannah John-Kamen and Lewis Pullman, are also teaming up with the original stars.

	Fox’s “X-Men” cast members are also crossing over into the MCU for “Doomsday.” The returning stars include Patrick Stewart, Ian McKellen, James Marsden, Kelsey Grammer, Alan Cumming, Rebecca Romijn and Channing Tatum.

title: ‘Black Panther 3’: David Jonsson to Play T’Challa’s Son as December 2028 Release Date Set
description:
Black Panther is back!

	David Jonsson has been cast as the new Black Panther and is playing T’Challa’s son in “Black Panther 3,”  out Dec. 15, 2028
body:
Black Panther is back!

	David Jonsson has been cast as the new Black Panther and is playing T’Challa’s son in “Black Panther 3,”  out Dec. 15, 2028. The film will follow Jonsson’s character, Prince T’Challa II, as he comes of age after he was introduced as a child in “Black Panther: Wakanda Forever.”

	Director Ryan Coogler will return for the third film, as well as Leticia Wright reprising her role as Shuri and Winston Duke as M’Baku. The news was announced at Marvel’s Comic-Con Hall H panel. 
	

	Wright took over as Black Panther from her late co-star Chadwick Boseman in “Black Panther: Wakanda Forever,” with Shuri becoming the eponymous superhero. Boseman, who portrayed T’Challa in the first “Black Panther,” died of colon cancerat age 43 in 2020, when Coogler was working on the sequel. The character T’Challa II was introduced as T’Challa and Nakia’s (Lupita Nyong’o) son in “Wakanda Forever.” 


	Jonsson recently starred in “Alien Romulus” and the adaptation of Stephen King’s “The Long Walk.” Wright told Variety in January 2023 after the release of “Wakanda Forever” that she thought the third film in the franchise was “already in the works.”

	“You know, we just had a terrific two years of bringing it out and everybody coming together to support it,” Wright said in the interview. “We need a little bit of a break, we need to regroup and Ryan needs to get back into the lab, so it’s going to take a little while, but we’re really excited for you guys to see that.”

	The first “Black Panther” movie, released in 2018, took in $1.3 billion at the worldwide box office, and starred Boseman, Wright, Lupita Nyong’o, Forrest Whitaker, Michael B. Jordan, Danai Gurira and Angela Bassett. It earned seven Oscar nominations, including best picture, the first superhero movie to do so. The film won three Oscars, including best costume design, best production design and best original score.
	

	“Black Panther: Wakanda Forever” grossed $859 million worldwide when it was released in 2022, and had one of the most profitable opening weekends post-pandemic, earning $331 million worldwide. The film was nominated for five Oscars, with Angela Bassett’s nomination for best supporting actress marking the first time any actor in a Marvel film was nominated for an Academy Award.

	Marvel fans won’t have to wait long to see Wright back in action as Black Panther, as she’s part of the sprawling “Avengers: Doomsday” cast. The film will hit theaters on Dec. 18.

title: ‘Coyote vs. Acme’ Director and Star Lana Condor on Finally Showing Their Film to the Fans at Comic-Con: ‘The Fight Was For a Good Reason’
description: If you went back to November 2023 and told “Coyote vs. Acme” director Dave Green that his Looney Toons legal comedy would make its debut at San Dieg
body:
If you went back to November 2023 and told “Coyote vs. Acme” director Dave Green that his Looney Toons legal comedy would make its debut at San Diego Comic-Con, he probably wouldn’t believe it. Of course, that’s largely because that’s when Green learned the film had been shelved by Warner Bros. Discovery as a tax write off.

	“For three years, I was lucky enough to make a movie about Wile E. Coyote, the most persistent, passionate, and resilient character of all time,” Green posted on X at the time after receiving the “devastating” news. “But in the spirit of Wile E. Coyote, resilience and persistence win the day.”
	

	And win the day they did. Ketchup Entertainment ultimately rescued the film and set it for theatrical release on Aug. 28. “Coyote vs. Acme” — an animated/live-action hybrid about Wile E. Coyote taking on the Acme Corporation for intentionally releasing defective products — will get its first public screening on Saturday night at Comic-Con.

	“I’ve waited so long to see their reaction. I feel like the years, to me, have [all led] up to tonight,” said Lana Condor, who stars in the film alongside Will Forte, John Cena and a bunch of Looney Tunes like Roadrunner, Tweety and Bugs Bunny. “I want so badly for them to love it, and I think they will. I’m so confident in that.”

	The most enduring image of the campaign to save “Coyote vs. Acme” was a lone protester dressed as Wile E. Coyote, holding a picket sign that read “Release Me” outside Warner Bros. Studios in the pouring rain.

	“We did a call to action, ‘Where are you? Reveal yourselves, we would love to invite you!'” Condor said. But Green confirmed the lone wolf never stepped forward. Still, the anonymous whistleblower’s legacy lives on as the “Coyote vs. Acme” team built one of his masks for last year’s Comic-Con panel.
	

	“We figured out how his costume was built, and it was made out of paper!” Green said excitedly.

	“Coyote vs. Acme” is heading to theaters while Warner Bros. is enduring yet another change of direction — this time, the impending merger with Paramount Skydance, which has many people in the industry on edge.

	But while the wider implications of the Warner-Paramount merger remain to be seen (especially after the merger’s delay), for tonight, the entire “Coyote vs. Acme” cast and crew have much to celebrate.

	“So many people stood up for a film they didn’t even see … which is exactly Wile’s entire journey throughout our entire film!” Condor said. “The reason that it’s going to come out at all, I firmly believe, is because of the fans. That was really incredible to experience. That’s why tonight, we’re so excited to screen it for the first time because this is what you fought for. I’m so confident that the fight was for a good reason.”

	The film’s script was penned by “May December” scribe Samy Burch from a story by James Gunn and Jeremy Slater. It is based on a 1990 New Yorker article by Ian Frazier.

	Watch the full conversation with Variety‘s Angelique Jackson above.

title: Ryan Gosling to Star in Marvel’s Ghost Rider Movie
description:
Ryan Gosling is finally joining the Marvel Cinematic Universe.

	The “Project Hail Mary” star will play Ghost Rider in a new standalone movie, Marve
body:
Ryan Gosling is finally joining the Marvel Cinematic Universe.

	The “Project Hail Mary” star will play Ghost Rider in a new standalone movie, Marvel Studios exec Kevin Feige announced onstage from Hall H at San Diego Comic Con. The film will be directed by Shawn Levy and is slated to release in 2028. 

	Levy is no stranger to the world of Marvel, most recently directing and producing the blockbuster “Deadpool & Wolverine” film. He and Gosling also recently collaborated on the upcoming “Star Wars: Starfighter,” which Levy also directed and in which Gosling stars. That film is due to release on May 28, 2027.
	

	“I’m having the greatest flashback vibes here, because I was here two years ago when we showed ‘Deadpool & Wolverine,'” Levy said upon taking the Hall H stage alongside Gosling and Feige. “I’ll never forget that night, because I was introduced to the greatest fans. Gosling is the absolute shit. I say that with tremendous respect. We spent a lot of time last year making ‘Starfighter,’ and the opportunity as Ryan started talking about this character, I was like, ‘Bro, let’s ride.’ We’ll see you in 2028!”


	Gosling will be the second actor to play the Spirit of Vengeance in a film after Nicolas Cage played the fiery motorcycle rider in two Sony movies. The character was also portrayed by Gabriel Luna as the Robbie Reyes version of the comic book character in the Marvel-ABC series “Agents of SHIELD.” Luna was set to reprise the role in a standalone series for Hulu, but that project was scrapped in 2019. 

	Cage first starred in Sony’s “Ghost Rider” movie in 2007, playing motorcycle stuntman Johnny Blaze. In the comics and his origin story movie, Johnny sells his soul to the devil Mephisto in order to cure his father’s cancer. As with any deal with the devil, Mephisto does cure Johnny’s dad, but he still dies in a stunt accident. Johnny then becomes bonded to a supernatural demon called the Spirit of Vengeance and is able to transform into a flaming, skeletal biker. He also has super-strength, wields fiery chain whips and can force someone to experience the emotional pain they’ve inflicted upon others with his Penance Stare. 
	

	Cage reprised his role for the 2011 sequel, “Ghost Rider: Spirit of Vengeance,” but reviews for both films were mostly negative.

	The rights to Ghost Rider reverted to Marvel Studios, which reinvented the character for the ABC TV show “Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.” Gabriel Luna played the Robby Reyes version of the character, who’s a younger, Latino man who takes on the Ghost Rider mantle.

	Gosling is having a major year after starring in “Project Hail Mary,” and he’ll join the Star Wars universe in next year’s “Starfighter” spinoff.

schema.headline: Ryan Gosling to Star in Marvel’s Ghost Rider Movie

body:
Amazon Prime Video has released a new teaser trailer for “Carrie,” the TV adaptation of Stephen King’s classic horror novel. All eight episodes of the series will debut on Oct. 7.

	The series is a “bold and timely reimagining of the story of misfit high-schooler Carrie White, who has spent her life in seclusion with her domineering mother,” the logline teases. “After her father’s sudden and untimely death, Carrie finds herself contending with the alien landscape of public high school, a bullying scandal that shatters her community, and the emergence of mysterious telekinetic powers.”
	

	Summer H. Howell will play Carrie White, with Siena Agudong as Sue Snell and Matthew Lillard as Principle Grayle. Also starring in the series are Samantha Sloyan as Margaret White, Alison Thornton as Chris Hargensen, Thalia Dudek as Emaline, Amber Midthunder as Miss Desjardin, Josie Totah as Tina, Arthur Conti as Billy and Joel Oulette as Tommy.

	Mike Flanagan serves as the writer, executive producer, showrunner and director, with Trevor Macy executive producing and Amazon MGM Studios producing.

	This is far from Howell’s first horror project, as she’s previously appeared in “Curse of Chucky,” “Cult of Chucky,” “Hunter Hunter,” “Spirit in the Blood,” “Time Cut,” “Harland Manor” and “Channel Zero.” Sloyan and Flanagan have been long-time collaborators, with Sloyan previously starring in Flanagan’s “The Haunting of Hill House,” “The Fall of the House of Usher,” “The Midnight Club,” “Midnight Mass” and “Hush.”
	

	“Carrie” will consist of eight episodes and was first reported to be in development in Oct. 2024. The series was officially greenlit by Amazon in April 2025. King’s novel was first adapted into an Oscar-nominated hit film in 1976, followed by a poorly received sequel in 1999, a television film in 2002 and a remake in 2013.

title: ‘Hadestown’ Brings Broadway’s Underworld to the Big Screen: Original Cast Members and Creator Anaïs Mitchell on Reconvening for a Smashing Cinema Event

body:
The gods themselves get mostly shoved out of the picture in “The Odyssey,” as has been noted by some filmgoers who wished Zeus or Poseidon got in on the action instead of just being talked about. But Hades, at least, has his day in another movie currently in theaters, which offers some serious interplay between men and immortals. It’s “Hadestown: The Musical,” the filming of one of the most acclaimed and successful Broadway musicals of the last decade. The hit show’s cinematic translation is predicted to make around $9 million at the U.S. box office this weekend, which would put it behind only the theatrical opening of the “Hamilton” film among grosses for a direct capture of a stage production. As it turns out, musical tragedy makes for perfectly fine summer counterprogramming after all, when the gods get to have their way.
	

	“Hadestown” is not typical Broadway fare, of course: André Robin De Shields, who won a Tony in 2020 for playing the god Hermes, says he considers it a “folk opera.” Nearly any description of the plot, which reenacts the ancient story of Orpheus and Eurydice, is going to make it sound a bit esoteric by modern tuner standards, even before tacking on Americana musician Anaïs Mitchell‘s unusually flavored, sung-through score. And yet the show has a massive cult, especially but not entirely among young people, that is at least as feverish in adoring intensity as “Hamilton’s.” It can only grow with the introduction into theaters of director Brett Sullivan’s brilliantly filmed adaptation, which is bound to draw untold numbers of newbies into its underworld, even as hardcore fans are bound to sign up for multiple trips before the movie’s scheduled one week in theaters is over.
	

	On the eve of the film’s release, Variety talked with Mitchell, Sullivan and several of the five original Broadway cast members who reunited for the movie — Reeve Carney, Eva Noblezada, Patrick Page and De Shields — about why “Hadestown” seems to have found a permanent foothold in American culture and what went in to making this rendering such a surprisingly indelible cinematic experience.

	Says Mitchell, “In this film, there was a really beautiful collaboration between Rachel Chavkin (the stage director) and Brett from Steam Motion, who directed the film, and they did a lot of close work on the edits and figuring out how to present the story. There’s so much emotional access to the characters because of the close-ups, and you can see things like a tear rolling down someone’s cheek or someone’s lip twitching that you wouldn’t be able to see from the audience. But you also never lose sight of the fact that it’s a stage show. There are enough shots where you’re seeing the stage in context of the audience, and seeing the beautiful theater, which is the Lyric Theatre on the West End.” Sullivan doesn’t shy completely away from offering long shots that incorporate the enthusiastic crowd, or even reaction shots, but mostly he stays locked into what’s happening on stage, so that it feels closer to a bona fide movie musical than something that sounds as reductionist as a “capture.”



	

					Patrick Page and Amber Gray in ‘Hadestown: The Musical’
									Bleecker Street and LD Entertainment
	



	The five original Broadway principals — also including Amber Gray, as Persephone — got the old gang back together and went into the West End production five weeks before the film was shot in front of three live audiences. Performances were filmed in quick succession on a Friday night, Saturday afternoon and Saturday evening; there was also closeup filming done of some of the numbers while an audience was not present, to afford the cameras some views that would have spoiled things for paying ticketgoers.

	Says Reeve, who plays Orpheus, “Watching the film, we can really feel the love that the creative team, including Brett and all the cameramen, have for the piece. Because the planning that went into it was a Herculean task, really. Every shot you see in the film, we only had one take at it. For the Friday night, Saturday matinee and Saturday evening performances, each time there were four to six cameras that were shooting simultaneously. And for each performance, the cameras were moved to an entirely different part of the theater. So the end result is that it looks so cinematic because (added up) it was like a 30-camera shoot.”
	

	There is some delayed gratification here. “There was a desire and an attempt to do this in the winter of 2022,” says Carney, “because Amber Gray, the first cast member to join the show, was about to leave the show, and so they were like, ‘This is our only chance to capture it with all of you guys.’ That didn’t end up working at that time, so we didn’t think it would ever happen. So when we got the call saying ‘Hey, we have another chance to do this, but the only way this is gonna work is if we bring you guys over to London during this cast changeover that’s happening,’ we were really grateful, because having a second chance really lit a fire under everyone’s butt to make sure we get this right.” He was ultimately glad they ended up waiting. “There’s something really magical about the Lyric Theatre in London that allowed for this capture to be something that I don’t think it would’ve been, exactly, at the Walter Kerr (in New York). The stage is three-quarters the size in London, which really lent itself beautifully to a cinematic experience.”



	

					Eva Noblezada, Andre De Shields and Reeve Carney in ‘Hadestown: The Musical’
									Bleecker Street and LD Entertainment
	



	For fans who have only lived with the cast album for the last seven years, getting to finally put a face to Patrick Page’s beyond-baritone voice will be a revelation. But even those who saw one of his hundreds of performances will find something new in the camera’s tight focus as he wavers on whether to let the mortal characters get their way or not.

	“The wonderful thing about the film is that it allows the audience member to participate in things that were always part of those performances, but which even sitting in the fourth or fifth row of the audience you might not catch,” Page says. “A close-up comes right in and reads the actor’s thoughts. So that’s where you have the depth of all of that experience of the five original players who have layers and layers of subtext and and relationship-building along with the words and the music. We always knew that was there, and I would sometimes try to tell other people who were performing in the show, ‘Well, do you know what actually happens in that moment?’ Because of course what actually happened in the moment only happened in my head, or between Amber’s eyes and my eyes, or in Andre’s turn of phrase, or whatever it was. And yet for us, those things were as real as the notations or the poetry.”
	

	De Shields insists the actors didn’t consciously tone anything down to adjust for the cameras getting close in. “It’s only in film that you have to be cautioned not to play to the camera, because in the theater the audience is the camera,” says the show’s Hermes. “So when the cameras were actually there, we didn’t adjust any attitudes or any focus. We just had to do what we knew and what we had been feeling, in some instances, for two, three, four, five years.”

	Page, being interviewed alongside De Shields, jumps in to say that he might have had his focus more tightly trained. “Now that I’m thinking, Andre, maybe the only difference is that when you’re doing it eight times a week, you know exactly what you do at every moment. But perhaps there are times where you don’t actually do it; you sort of pretend to do it. Whereas on film, you know, it’s ‘I’ve gotta actually do this now or that damn camera’s gonna catch me. I can’t cheat.'”

	“I never cheated!” protests De Shields.

	“Oh, I saw you,” Page retorts, as they both laugh.

	No relationship developed over the course of the original production quite like the one between Carney and Noblezada, who are now married. As they speak beside one another on their couch at home, with occasional cameos from their dog, Noblezada is wearing a “Reeva” T-shirt, reflecting how much fans of the couple have enjoyed the real-life shipping that went on off-stage as well as on it.

	“Reeva… Somebody gave this to me as a gift,” she says. “I love it.”

	“We sleep in these shirts at night,” cracks Carney.

	“I did not sleep in this, just to be clear,” says Noblezada, setting the record straight. “I mean, we’re very grateful that people love the show and are big supporters of Reeva, individually and also together, because without that support we couldn’t really do what we do.”

	It’s safe to say they did not let the fact that “Hadestown” is a romantic tragedy stand as a bad omen for their own burgeoning relationship?

	“I don’t view ‘Hadestown’ as a tragedy,” counters Carney. “I view it as a piece designed to empower and embolden people to make a different decision and to choose a different ending. I see it as very optimistic and it’s a very hopeful piece, even though it is based upon a Greek tragedy. Everyone can have a different perspective, which is great, too. But I think that’s part of why young people keep coming back to it: I think deep down they know that they can change the world. I think it resonates with all age groups,” he adds, “but in terms of it resonating with young people in particular, I think it’s because it’s important to not forget who you were as a child, in order to make the changes in the world that our world so desperately needs.”
	



	

					Eva Noblezada and Reeve Carney in ‘Hadestown: The Musical’
									Bleecker Street and LD Entertainment
	



	Carney admits he did spend a moment or three thinking about how it might be difficult to revisit the intensity of the show after being out of it for a good spell. “Yes, there was a bit of that hesitation,” he admits. “I was the last one to leave the show, and even for me it had been a year and a half between when I left the show and coming back into it. But I had a lot of amazing communication with Rachel Chavkin and Anaïs Mitchell about what exactly they wanted for this version of ‘Hadestown,’ because we had all performed such different versions of the character over the years. And that was really crucial in terms of getting all of us on the same page, because I knew we only had three performances to capture this. Once I got locked in with that, the only thing I said to them is, ‘I think I know where we’re going with this, and if that’s the case, I cannot have the haircut that I had in 2019.’ There’s so much that costume and hair and makeup informs to the audience about a character before they even say a word. So I was like, ‘All right. I know what we’re doing — but I gotta change the hair.’ That was my only non-negotiable.”

	Noblezada, who has many of the most emotionally wreching moments in the show, wasn’t worried about any difficulty in finding all of that again after having had an extended break. “The good thing is, we don’t have to start from scratch. We have so much to pull from because the inner world of ‘Hadestown’ that we live in is so rich and so real. I mean, anybody who’s facing those issues would react with those emotions. And so you just have to know how to drop into your character’s body, and the world of ‘Hadestown’ — the lyrics, the blocking, the story, the pacing of it all — does the rest of it for you. I mean, it’s really like you get on a rollercoaster, and you know that you’re gonna have that almost vertical drop at a really high amount of speed, and you just have to strap down and lock in.

	“It’s not difficult for me to get emotional,” Noblezada adds. “I’m a very emotional person. I’m a quintuple Pisces. I’m a rising Gemini, with the two faces, which means I was destined to be an actor. But I also think that Eurydice’s story has to be deeply emotional and tragic because she falls in love, and then everything’s taken away from her, and then she makes a really big choice that affects her life and her future. So it’s not easy to feel those every night, but it’s easy to get into it.”
	



	

					Eva Noblezada and the fates in ‘Hadestown’
									Bleecker Street and LD Entertainment
	



	Whatever adjustments the stage-to-film translation did or didn’t require of the cast, it was a normal day’s work for Sullivan, who is certainly foremost among the directors doing these live stage captures for cinematic special engagements. He’s done about a dozen of them to date, including big-screen versions of “Miss Saigon” (on which he actually worked with Noblezada, 10 years ago), “Waitress,” “Kinky Boots,” “Frozen,” “Aladdin,” “Kiss Me Kate” and “Starlight Express.” “Literally tomorrow I deliver the ‘Stranger Things’ musical, which we shot on Broadway for Netflix. That was almost the other end of the spectrum, a very effects-heavy show, and trying to relay live magic onto the screen was a different challenge.”

	Sullivan has seen the change in attitude in the industry from a time in which there were questions about whether cinematic translations would hog all the interest that might otherwise go to keeping the ongoing stage productions going. “We tried it out with ‘Newsies’ with Disney quite a while ago [in 2017] and Tom Schumacher, who was heading up Disney theatrical, was like, ‘Let’s try this and see what happens.’ As it turns out, when the film did its event cinema thing, they got another couple of tours booked off the back of it just because the interest just got so wide again. That was a little bit of a proof in the pudding that, hey, these things can actually get the news out there, so to speak, and these things can co-exist.”

	Some of the challenges in doing a “capture” are more obvious than others. “I mean, when you go to the theater, you’re basically watching a wide shot all night, and your eyes can go wherever they want to. And we’re making choices for you for the screen, including who to look at, at what particular point in time, through the editing or the close-ups. ?” Knowing full well that obviously it’s a live thing, you want to honor that and be truthful to the show as much as possible. But there are some film conventions that we have to lean into. It’s a dance, isn’t it?
	

	“‘Stop Making Sense’ for me was the film that made me do what I do,” the director continues. “And I always wondered when I watched that, when I was probably 13, how did they get those shots close on stage, as well as the wide shots? I studied that thing backwards, and really that has become the template for me artistically: We need to see the actor’s eyes, and we also need to see the spectacle. ‘Stop Making Sense’ did that just so cleverly, so that’s been my benchmark for how to convey something live in an interesting way.”



	

					Director Brett Sullivan
									Bleecker Street and LD Entertainment
	



	Of what is unique about capturing “Hadestown,” Sullivan says, “The single set helped us, because the set doesn’t have traditional wings. The band is taking the space of traditional wings in a theater, which is great. It means we can shoot across, which gave us a sense of, like, the camera’s not always at the front. We’re getting into the sides, which helped with kind of the visual interest. And we have a lot of deep two-shots where there’s someone in the foreground and someone in the background, and we’re racking (focus) between the two. I was like, ‘OK, let’s reduce the cuts somehow. Let’s find the angles where we’ve always got a background person, or we’ve always got connections.’ So there’s all working in triangles, where someone’s listening and reacting to what the other person is singing, and we can try and make that visually interesting without cutting. So a lot of it was trying to search for these deep twos when we were designing the shots.”

	One unexpected adjustment that had to be made: allowing for Page’s injury to his foot, which has him wearing a large boot and carry a cane for the entirety of the show. It’s not something that the director shoots around; he and Persephone still have a tender dance number toward the end of the show.

	“Patrick had a wild ride,” says Mitchell. “You might have heard that he was injured during the rehearsal process, and that’s why he ended up in the live capture with this big boot on one of his legs. All of the actors actually were returning to the role after several years away from it, and partly they were falling back into their muscle memory, and then partly they had to kind of come at it in a new way, but most of all Patrick, because literally his dance moves had to be different and his blocking hit different because of his situation. But I feel like you feel them all authentically in their selves at the time of the taping, taking on these characters again with the added experience of six years of life that happened in between when we opened on Broadway and 2025.”
	

	What’s the appeal that leads to multiple viewings of the stage production (and now, presumably, the film)? Sullivan says: “I would have to say that Anais’ music is just so good that that’s people’s entry point into it; the staying power of those songs is so effective. I mean, the last song in the show, I tear up every single time I hear it — that we’re gonna sing it again, even though we know the ending. … And there’s some universal truths that run through it. Some of it seems political as well about how the times have kind of shaped some of these things, when you listen to it. ‘The Wall’ was written before the whole discourse about the wall (that subsequently became a focus in real life for Donald Trump, as it prophetically was for Hades in the show). There’s a lot of things that resonate right now in the world as we search for the truth in various means.”

	Page feels one moment in the script sums up the pull of the show… and it’s not one of Hades’ lines. “I think it’s in that one little toast of Orpheus’. I think it’s the tension between ‘the world we dream about and the one we live in now,’ and it’s that tension that we live in that I think attracts everyone to it — the possibility, and how do we get there? Because that tension isn’t somebody’s fault. But it’s a real thing, a real conflict. It’s a real paradox between what we wish could be and what is. And that, I think, is what keeps people in it. What do you think it is?”

	Says De Shields: “To speak in the current vernacular, I think the audience feels, ‘I’m finally being seen.’ Simply that.”

	Mitchell found herself being surprised by elements of her own show when she was able to suddenly study them on immaculately captured film. “I’ve seen it so many times that it’s hard to get a response sometimes because I know it so well,” she allows. “But there are moments that hit me different emotiuonally. Like, this version of Eva singing ‘Flowers’ feels so raw and huge and intimate. That felt like something new. And then I guess, there’s something about the fact that when you see it on film, you’re in the story, but then you’re also in the experience of the audience experiencing the story, you know? That feels like the story is not just the story; the story is what it has come to mean for people.

	“I’ve seen the show a million times, but there were little things that struck me, like the way that a shadow of a character hits the set in a certain moment, or the subtle choreography of the Fates or the workers in the background when they’re kind of listening to the principal actors, and they’re moving in a way that supports the emotion of the singer. It’s subtle, but it’s always present, and I found it easier to focus on that in the film version. Because a lot of times I’m just obsessed with words. I’m, like, always, ‘How is it being phrased? What does the language sound like?’ But there’s this whole ‘nother level of what’s going on that is visual, image-based, impressionistic in a way.
	

	“I think that sort of hit home a little more with this film: a sense of mystery for me, again, where I’m like, ‘Oh, I have no idea what this thing is.’ As many years of my life as I’ve put into it, I have no idea what this thing is or what it means to people. It’s got its own life. It’s moving around the world on its own legs.”



	

					NEW YORK, NEW YORK – JULY 13: (L-R) Anaïs Mitchell, Reeve Carney, and Eva Noblezada visit the Empire State Building on July 13, 2026 in New York City. (Photo by Roy Rochlin/Getty Images for Empire State Realty Trust)
									Getty Images for Empire State Re
	



	Mitchell’s key points of identification with her handiwork have shifted. “When I started writing it in my early 20s. I for sure identified with Orpheus at that time, and Eurydice, and the idealism. I still do at some level, but I’m now in my 40s and I identify much more with the story of the older marriage [between Hades and Persephone] — is there a chance for redemption with these people that have been together for years and years? And I relate to the role of Hermes, who has to retell this sad story again and again and be the storyteller. There’s something about all those characters that are present in this story that has allowed me to stay alive with it, from what I passed through my early 20s to being like, ‘I’m still interested in it.’ Like, I’m still interested, now, in what’s going through Hades’ head here.”

	The show opened on Broadway in 2019, but in a different way of thinking, it is celebrating both a 10th anniversary and 20th anniversary this year. It was 2016 when “Hadestown” first opened off-Broadway, but 2006 when Mitchell first began doing an early version of it with musician friends in folk clubs, like McCabe’s in Santa Monica.
	

	“Someone else mentioned that to me the other day — the 2016, 2006 (anniversary) thing — and it hadn’t crossed my mind,” says Mitchell. “It’s crazy to me to think that I’ve been living alongside of this piece in one way or another for 20 years, which is almost half my life. But the story for me is that it’s still alive, and the fact that we get to keep telling this story night after night on Broadway and the West End, and that we now have this film document so that we can reach folks who wouldn’t make it to the theater otherwise. It’s not a reenactment of what it was in 2016. Obviously the text is evolving less than it did 10 years ago, but as a piece of theater, I think people are still finding new ways to present it. And actually, a lot of young people are putting it on. We released the rights for high schools, and that’s been really moving, to see young people find themselves in the story and in the characters. I get all kinds of requests from high schools, like, ‘Can we have nine Fates?’ ‘Can we have 100 workers?’ ‘Can we have everyone non-binary?’ It’s very cool to see what they’re doing.”

	Carney has a thought about what resonates for all demographics about the show. “As actors, one of our jobs is to constantly be expanding our capacity for empathy,” he says. “Because there are times when we can draw from our own life, but there are times when you may not have exactly experienced something, but if you can empathize with it, then you can put that into the character. I think empathy is something we need more of, and I think the show, hopefully, will continue to encourage more of that. Because I, for one, do not think that empathy is… what is the word that was used recently?” He searches for the language Elon Musk made famous. “I don’t think empathy is a detriment in any way, or a weakness.” Even in hardboiled Hadestown, that would probably get a murmur of assent.

title: Fantasia International Film Festival Awards: Hanna Bergholm’s ‘Nightborn’ Wins Top Honor
description:

body:
Hanna Bergholm’s “Nightborn” has won the top honor at this year’s Fantasia International Film Festival juried awards.

	“Nightborn” was awarded the prestigious Cheval Noir trophy for best film. Seidi Haarla, who stars opposite Rupert Grint in the film, was also awarded best actress. Kasper Kalle’s “No Rest for the Wicked” also took home two statues for best director and best actor for Pilou Asbæk.


	Andrea Corsini’s “Ferine” also took home two top honors: best cinematography for Fabrizio La Palombara and best score for the legendary Pino Donaggio.
	

	See the full winners list — along with jury statements — below.

	2026 Cheval Noir Awards

	Best Film

	Nightborn (Finland/Lithuania/France/U.K.), dir. Hanna Bergholm

	“‘It sucks my body, it destroys my career.’ When the anticipated birth and the child who should be loved become the most threatening presence to a mother, she fails to accept the child into her world. To her, the child is not a ‘him,’ but an ‘it.’ This psychological thriller explores the destruction of a woman’s daily life- where everything around her could be reality, or merely an illusion. Ultimately, when she gives up everything and steps into the ‘child’s’ world, we finally discover the “most adorable” child in the world. The suspense keeps you glued to the screen every single second, and the emotion in the ending is bittersweet — making you smile yet feel profoundly sad. This film will stay with us for a long time.”

	Best Director

	Kasper Kalle, No Rest for the Wicked (Denmark/Faroe Islands/Iceland)
	

	“Like the captain of a sailing vessel, the director is the creative force that unites the crew, bringing all the creative elements and storytelling emotion together on the screen, and one film did that big time for both audiences and the jury. For his skillful helming of a beautifully dark period piece that reveals the discovery and acceptance of identity through a love story, the jury awards Best Director to Kasper Kalle.”

	Best Screenplay

	Edwin, Eka Kurniawan, and Daishi Matsunaga, Sleep No More (Japan/Germany/Singapore/Indonesia), dir. Edwin

	“For a genuinely original storytelling vision that draws Asian folklore, humor, and workers rights, and extreme body horror into a story of family reunification, the jury awards the Best Screenplay Award to Edwin, Eka Kurniawan, Daishi Matsunaga.”

	Best Cinematography

	Fabrizio La Palombara, CCS, Ferine (Italy), dir. Andrea Corsini

	“For its technical and artistic skill, a carefully measured use of the anamorphic format, varied lighting and precise camera composition that wonderfully reflects the narrative and the amazing brutalist Production Design and radical swing character arcs that throttle the audience. For its look that pays homage to the greats of Italian horror while adding its own stamp to a modern genre film while constantly reinventing itself visually, the jury presents the Cheval Noir for Best Cinematography to Fabrizio La Palombara, CCS.”

	Best Editing

	Soichi Ueno, Beasts Clutching at Straws (Japan), dir. Hideo Jojo

	“We are honored to be the first Fantasia jury to present the new award for best film editing. My former boss and co-editor Orson Welles once said that editing is the last stop on the long road between the dream in the filmmaker’s head, and the public to whom that dream is addressed. The editor focuses that dream into reality. For its dynamic pacing, masterful control of non-linear construction, and clever use of imaginative transitions, while never losing track of the characters and story, the jury presents the award for outstanding editing to Soichi Ueno.”

	Best Score

	Pino Donaggio, Ferine (Italy), dir. Andrea Corsini

	“Music has the power to soothe, shock and enchant the viewer as it accompanies the characters through the narrative. For the jury, the dramatic music of one colorful, ravenous film stood out, and it marks the return of a revered screen composer- one who might be familiar to fans of classic films like Don’t Look Now and Carrie. The musical artistry of this 84 year-old legend can be heard in two Fantasia films this year, and the jury is thrilled to present the award for outstanding score to Pino Donaggio.”
	

	Outstanding Performance Award

	Seidi Haarla, Nightborn (Finland/Lithuania/France/U.K.), dir. Hanna Bergholm

	“Genre film is built on risk-taking performances, and this year the jury was completely captivated by a transcendent portrayal of a very different kind of determined mother. With dark humor, astonishing physicality, and heart-wrenching body horror, this actor brings to life a woman struggling beneath the weight of her family’s expectations (and her own) as she unravels and transforms before our eyes.”

	Outstanding Performance Award

	Pilou Asbæk, No Rest for the Wicked (Denmark/Faroe Islands/Iceland), dir. Kasper Kalle

	“Genre cinema has always been drawn to mysterious strangers, but few arrivals have felt as quietly transformative as this one. Through effortless magnetism, and extraordinary emotional precision, this actor crafts a character who belongs as much to the sea as the shore. Every movement, every silence, every knot tied and glance exchanged reveals a soul shaped by freedom, isolation, and the courage to embrace his own identity.”

	Special Mention of the Jury: Full Ensemble

	Hot Spot (Sweden/Greece/Norway/Poland), dir. Agnieszka Smoczyńska

	“The jury wishes to recognize the achievement of an ensemble cast of individual performers and the monsters are pretty cool too. The story and world building of this film is conveyed by the core characters- a family that communicates without speaking and with intense physicality that transforms them all- and by the supporting performances of the extras- such as a group of religious refugees who move and breathe together in unison. For its exceptionally nuanced collective performance, the jury awards a Special Mention to the ensemble cast of Hot Spot.”

	Special Mention of the Jury: Special Practical Effects

	Jabrik Hellworker, Benedictus A.K., Rizal, and Issei Oda, Sleep No More (Japan/Germany/Singapore/Indonesia), dir. Edwin

	“One film impressed the jury with its handmade practical effects and the VFX they engage with — an angry and ravenous hair monster, a character that grows back missing limbs — all beautifully integrated into the surreal nightmare of the story. For its amazingly original use of practical effects, a Cheval Noir Special Mention goes to Sleep No More.”
	

	Jury President: Youngjoo Suh (founder and CEO of Finecut Co., Ltd. and producer).Jury: Catherine Corcoran (actor, writer, producer, and festival programmer), Karim Hussain (cinematographer, director, and screenwriter), Bob Murawski (Oscar-winning film editor and co-founder of Grindhouse Releasing), and Junnie Punter (journalist with Variety, Toronto Film Critics Association, producer, and editor at Musicworks Magazine).

	2026 New Flesh Competition for Best First Feature

	New Flesh Award for Best First Feature

	Mum, I’m Alien Pregnant (New Zealand), dirs. THUNDERLIPS

	“This debut feature was a wild ride from start to finish, with zany design complementing its shock, horror, and humor. The filmmakers have conceived a world that is both funny and extreme, navigating themes of bodily autonomy for both males and females through the playful and the monstrous. This year’s New Flesh competition winner — and best alien penis of the festival — goes to Mum, I’m Alien Pregnant.”

	Special Mention of the Jury: Best Performance

	Dilnaz Kurmangali and Ayan Utepburgen, Sicko (Kazakhstan), dir. Aitore Zholdaskali

	“We are delighted to present an honorable mention for best performance to these two leads. This male and female duo navigated the film’s tonal shifts between horror and comedy with ease. Balancing each other’s intensity to create a memorable dynamic, their performances made an impact, bringing humanity and dimension to unlikable characters just trying to survive in a gritty, complex world. The honorable mention for best performance goes to Dilnaz Kurmangali and Ayan Utepburgen from Sicko.”

	Jury President: Brandon Hill (Senior Director of Acquisitions and Co-Productions, Lionsgate).Jury: Jasper Basch (partner and head of distribution of Greenwich Entertainment, former head of theatrical at IFC, and former head of distribution at Variance), Julien Fonfrède (director, producer, screenwriter, critic, and festival programmer at Festival du nouveau cinema), Markus Keuschnigg (film critic, writer, and co-founder and artistic director of Slash Filmfestival Vienna), and Hillary Webber (production manager for Film Tampa Bay and industry programmer at Gasparilla International Film Festival).

	2026 Satoshi Kon Award for Excellence in Animation

	Satoshi Kon Award for Best Animated Feature

	Blaise (France), dirs. Jean-Paul Guigue and Dimitri Planchon

	“We were struck by how this film transforms social anxiety, people-pleasing, and painfully uncomfortable silences into something hilarious. Its flat, collage-like, strangely realistic world perfectly reflects these awkward characters who are constantly trying to fit into everyone else’s expectations. What impressed us most is that beneath the comedy is a film full of empathy, reminding us that we’re all a little awkward sometimes and through that humor, it reminds us that finding the confidence to be ourselves and sometimes simply saying no isn’t always easy. The Award for Best Feature goes to Dimitri Planchon and Jean-Paul Guigue for Blaise.”

	Special Mention of the Jury

	Cherry and Virgin (Japan), dir. Masanao Kawajiri

	“The honorable mention goes to a film whose characters felt so authentic, with emotions that are honest, messy, and relatable. It’s a story with so much heart, and one where the animation technique and storytelling couldn’t be a better fit. Bringing two completely different visual styles together is no small feat, and this film makes it look effortless, it’s playful, seamless and a joy to watch. It beautifully captures what it feels like to navigate insecurity, vulnerability, and human connection. The honorary mention goes to Masanao Kawajiri for Cherry and Virgin.”
	

	Satoshi Kon Award for Best Short Film — Gold

	Jeem 1983 (Lebanon), dir. Jorj Abou Mhaya

	“A life in the arts can be a struggle. But it’s nothing compared to a life living among war. Using art to escape into a reality that imagines beauty where there is none is one of the most powerful statements art can make. A glimpse into a world of Arabic animation that rarely gets to the west in festivals like Fantasia, and hopefully more submissions will be encouraged by this. A young boy travels through 1983 Beirut suspending the horrors and using fantasy for a momentary reprieve. Did we mention Goldorak shows up? The Gold Satoshi Kon Award for Excellence in Animation goes to Jori Abou Mhaya’s Jeem 1983.”

	Satoshi Kon Award for Best Short Film — Silver

	Fingerbang (South Korea), dir. Kim Yeon-woo

	“Plenty of films can be surreal, but this one makes you believe in the relationship. Through the most unusual premise, it explores how obsession and longing can distort love, reminding us that the things we desire most can ultimately consume us. The Silver Satoshi Kon Award for Excellence in Animation goes to Kim Yeonwoo’s Fingerbang.”

	Satoshi Kon Award for Best Short Film — Bronze

	The End of the End (U.S./South Korea), dir. Junar Kim

	“Executed with an astounding atmosphere through low-key lighting, theatrical staging this film transforms the contemplation of death into a breathtaking work of art. The animation perfectly complements its contemplative pace, drawing us deeper into its haunting world. 	“Our choice for special mention goes to a film we found bold, distinct, and full of Cronenbergian chutzpah. This feature manages to simultaneously be a post-COVID cautionary tale about bug addiction and a celebration of kink. For its sheer itch factor and use of mixed media, this year’s special mention goes to Angus Silver’s Insectasy.”

            Natalya Scudder -- a star on season 7 and season 8 of "Below Deck" -- says she spent the night in disgusting digs at a detention center before being deported from the USA.
      
    
            We spoke to the reality star and influencer earlier this week ... and she told us all about her nightmarish experience -- which began when she was detained by authorities over photos she took in the USA during her last visit.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            She says she was told cashing in on the snaps as she had meant she needed a different kind of visa than the one she applied for ... at which point she says they took her to a dirty room and told her she'd be staying for anywhere between 1 and 5 days.
      

            Watch the clip to hear Natalya describe the rough accommodations ... from the lack of towels to the dirty bedding.
      
    
            Eventually -- after a rough night -- she says she was taken in for an interview and promptly deported ... sent back on a plane to Australia. She says it was a 17-hour flight there, 30-40 hours in lockup and a prompt 17-hour flight home.
      
    
            While she loves America, Natalya says authorities are cracking down ... and she warns her fellow influencers to be very careful when traveling through the country.
      
    
            After all, they don't want to end up below decency like these authorities allegedly subjected her to!
